_note: English translations of selected rows of firegap_dataset/data/facts_all.csv (original text in Russian, column fact_ru). Source, page and 'verified' come from the CSV unchanged; only fact/caveat/where are translated here.

G01.fact: The assumption that 'microgravity is safer' relied on tests in still air. In real compartments ventilation strongly feeds the flame, so that safety margin may not hold.

G02.fact: At low flow speeds (micro- and partial gravity) some materials burn at lower O₂ than in normal gravity (flammability map, fig. 8).

G03.fact: In low gravity materials ignite more easily, because there is no natural convection cooling the surface.

G04.fact: With slow flow a flame can spread against the flow, i.e. the opposite of normal gravity (depends on flow speed).

G06.fact: On oxygen-vs-flow-speed maps, radiative losses dominate at very low speeds and the flame goes out. The minimum O₂ and the maximum spread rate lie near 10 cm/s, typical of spacecraft ventilation.
G06.caveat: A qualitative diagram (fig. 8); exact values depend on the material.
G06.where: p. 31, Highlights and Lessons Learned: Low-Stretch Flames

G13.fact: SoFIE was planned to supply air at 0–30 cm/s (the spacecraft ventilation range) and to study 'Space Exploration Atmospheres'.

G19.fact: SAMS and MAMS have continuously measured vibratory and quasi-steady (<0.01 Hz) accelerations on the ISS at 21 locations since 2001; the PIMS project collects the data.

G20.fact: The guide describes reduced and partial gravity only qualitatively: it contains no numerical data for the Moon or Mars.
G20.caveat: Numbers must be taken from other NTRS reports.

X01.fact: Test 1 (upward flame propagation): a material passes if three samples each burn less than 6 in (15 cm) and the flame is not transferred by burning debris. One failed sample fails the material.
X01.caveat: One vertical geometry (flame upward). It is a burn/no-burn length threshold, not a spread rate or a risk.

X02.fact: Test 1 conditions are set as the 'worst case' for pressure, temperature, O₂ concentration and thickness. The text gives no specific numbers; each project chooses them.
X02.caveat: So the standard has no single 'safe' O₂/pressure range.

X09.fact: The word 'gravity' does not appear anywhere in the 1998 standard: all tests run in Earth gravity, vertically upward. It contains no data for microgravity, the Moon or Mars.
X09.caveat: This is the 1998 version. Later editions (6001B, 2016) are mentioned in Ferkul 2026; their text was not opened.

X10.fact: Flames may be more dangerous on the Moon: spread rate as a function of gravity peaks near lunar gravity, and the minimum O₂ concentration for burning lies near lunar g (theory and related work).
X10.caveat: Theory and model plus aircraft and centrifuge experiments; O₂-limit numbers vs gravity should be taken from the graph in Olson et al. 2024.

X11.fact: NASA FM2: a 14.4 L chamber on the lunar surface (delivered by a commercial lander), four 20 cm fabric samples, lunar gravity 0.165 g, several O₂ levels. Goal: the first flame-spread measurements on the Moon. The source has no results.

X12.fact: Thin cellulose on the KC-135 aircraft: 0.2–0.4 atm, gravity 0.1 g, 0.16 g (Moon) and 0.38 g (Mars), widths 1/2/4 cm; observed spread rates and pyrolysis lengths were roughly proportional to the gravity level (upward flame).
X12.caveat: Spread-rate numbers from the paper's tables were not extracted; take them from the PDF first.

X13.fact: For downward spread, partial-gravity data were previously limited to Sacksteder and T'ien (0.05–1.0 g, 5 cm Kimwipes samples); downward spread rate peaks at partial g.
X13.caveat: The 1994 original paper was not opened.

X14.fact: KC-135 programme: partial gravity 0.1–1 g, both directions (up and down) on thin fuels; steady spread rates and approximate extinction boundaries were measured at different pressures and widths.

X15.fact: Direct partial-gravity tests are few because there are no long-duration facilities; results suggest lunar and Martian gravity may increase concurrent flame-spread tendency, with a 'sweet spot' near lunar gravity (centrifuge studies).
X15.caveat: A review and position paper, not primary measurements.

X16.fact: Parabolic-flight tests: limiting O₂ concentration (LOC) and spread rate along wire insulation as functions of gravity, O₂, flow speed and insulation thickness; the introduction notes earlier work found the LOC minimum and the spread peak at partial gravity.

X17.fact: Reduced pressure partly mimics low gravity for PMMA cylinders: lowering pressure slows flame spread towards what is expected in low g; normal-g and microgravity (BASS-II) data correlate.
X17.caveat: An approximation, not a measurement in partial g.

X18.fact: Atmospheres of 21–34% O₂ and 8–14.7 psia: at 30% O₂ spread over hair is more than ten times faster than at 21%; for upward spread 1 g is faster than 0 g; pressure has little effect on flame-tip speed; opposed flow cannot be generalised to the Moon or Mars.
X18.caveat: The material is human hair, not cabin lining.

X19.fact: BASS-II data from the ISS (PMMA and cotton/fiberglass): extinction happens at conditions where materials burn at lower O₂ in microgravity than on Earth.
X19.caveat: No numbers in the abstract; a qualitative conclusion matching our BASS-II data.

X20.fact: For cellulose in opposed flow, the Earth LOI is 16.5% O₂; with flow typical of spacecraft ventilation (5–20 cm/s) the flame survives even at 14% O₂. Test 1 is not always conservative.
X20.caveat: Confirms the ISS guide's point about ~10 cm/s.

X22.fact: Exploration atmosphere: 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa) and 34% O₂; previously 8.0 psia (55.2 kPa) and 32% was recommended. The Shuttle was certified for 10.2 psia (70.3 kPa) and 26.5% O₂.
X22.caveat: The lunar/Mars atmosphere is not final (per Garbino 2022, parameters are not approved).

X23.fact: For an 8.2 psia / 34–40% O₂ atmosphere, material flammability is named the hardest obstacle: about 70% of assessed ECLSS subsystems would need material changes, many not yet developed.
X23.caveat: Confirms that 34–40% O₂ at ~56 kPa is an operating region where our dataset has no solid-material tests.

X24.fact: Apollo and Gemini: 5.0 psi, 100% O₂. For Artemis this is called an unacceptable flammability risk.
X24.caveat: The pressure of the Apollo 1 ground-test fire was different (see the Senate report); this refers to the in-flight atmosphere.

X26.fact: JAXA's FLARE experiment in Kibo (MSPR): flame spread over flat samples, rods and insulated wires at low opposed and concurrent flow; measures the minimum limiting O₂ concentration in microgravity (MLOC).
X26.caveat: The page gives no MLOC numbers.

X31.fact: 'Fire on the Moon' slides: research priority is to obtain partial-gravity data; 34% O₂ plus lunar gravity may be a very challenging condition for fire safety.
